pages.title: Which atom pulls a shared pair more strongly?

blocks.text: In H₂, identical atoms share a bonding pair equally. In HCl, the two atoms do not attract that pair equally. We need a way to compare attraction inside a chemical bond.
Electronegativity addresses this bonded situation. It should not be confused with the energy change when an isolated gaseous atom gains an electron.

pages.transition: Give the shared-pair attraction a clear definition.

pages.title: Define electronegativity in context

blocks.text: Electronegativity is an atom’s tendency to attract the shared electron pair towards itself in a chemical bond. The comparison concerns a bonded atom in its chemical environment.
Unlike ionisation enthalpy, it is not directly measured as one unique isolated-atom energy change. Different scales assign comparative numbers; the familiar Pauling scale is dimensionless.

“Shared” does not necessarily mean “equally shared.” Two bonded atoms may attract the same pair unequally. Electronegativity compares that tendency; partial-charge symbols describe the resulting uneven electron distribution.

pages.transition: Use effective nuclear attraction to understand the across-period change.

pages.title: Explain the across-period trend

blocks.text: Across a main-group period, decreasing size and increasing effective nuclear attraction generally strengthen attraction for a shared pair. Electronegativity therefore generally increases from left to right.
Fluorine is the most electronegative element on the usual scale. A high value means strong attraction in a bond; it does not mean a neutral fluorine atom already carries a negative charge.

pages.transition: A group comparison introduces extra shells and shielding.

pages.title: Explain the down-group trend

blocks.text: Down a group, the valence region grows larger and inner electrons provide more shielding. The nucleus attracts a bonding pair less effectively at the larger distance, so electronegativity generally decreases.
Fluorine attracts a shared pair more strongly than chlorine in the general group comparison. This trend is different from the F/Cl exception for electron gain enthalpy.

pages.transition: Translate unequal attraction into partial charge separation.

pages.title: Translate unequal attraction into polarity

blocks.text: In HCl, chlorine draws electron density towards itself. Chlorine has a partial negative charge δ− and hydrogen a partial positive charge δ+. The pair is still shared in a polar covalent bond.
The symbols δ+ and δ− mean fractional charge separation. They do not claim complete electron transfer into free H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in an isolated HCl molecule.

pages.transition: Identical atoms provide the simplest non-polar reference.

pages.title: Use equal atoms as a comparison

blocks.text: H₂ and Cl₂ have no electronegativity difference between their two atoms, so the bonding pair is shared symmetrically. Their individual bonds are non-polar.

An unlike-atom bond can be polar even when a larger molecule’s total dipole cancels by symmetry. Bond polarity and whole-molecule polarity are separate questions; molecular shape is studied with bonding.

pages.transition: Connect these bonding tendencies with metallic and non-metallic character.

pages.title: Relate electronegativity to metallic character

blocks.text: Elements that easily lose valence electrons tend to be metallic and less electronegative. Stronger attraction for shared electrons is generally associated with non-metallic character.

Thus across-period trends in metallic character and electronegativity usually run in opposite directions. Both can be explained through effective attraction and outer-shell structure, rather than unrelated memorised arrows.

pages.transition: Keep the three electron-related quantities distinct by their definitions.

pages.title: Compare three different quantities

blocks.text: Ionisation enthalpy concerns X(g)→X⁺(g)+e⁻. Electron gain enthalpy concerns X(g)+e⁻→X⁻(g). Electronegativity concerns attraction for a shared pair in a bond.

The first two are enthalpy changes with energy units and specified gas-phase processes. Electronegativity is a relative bonded-atom measure. Similar trends do not make the definitions interchangeable.

pages.transition: Apply the trends to a particular bond comparison.

pages.title: Use a trend without inventing a numerical cutoff

blocks.text: Teacher application: compare the bonds H–F and H–Cl qualitatively. F is more electronegative than Cl, so it attracts bonding electrons more strongly; the electron sharing is more unequal in H–F.

Do not treat an arbitrary electronegativity difference as a universal exact boundary between ionic and covalent bonding. Actual bond character changes continuously and also depends on the chemical environment.

Compare C–C and C–Cl qualitatively. The identical carbon atoms have no electronegativity difference in C–C. In C–Cl, Cl attracts the shared density more strongly, so the bond is polar with Cl δ−. No full electron transfer is implied.

pages.transition: Review the interpretation without inventing universal numerical cutoffs.

pages.title: Explain attraction rather than repeat arrows

blocks.text: Electronegativity increases generally across periods and decreases down groups. Interpret a value only in a bonding context, then use the difference to reason about unequal sharing.
Keep partial charge distinct from a full ionic charge, and bond polarity distinct from molecular polarity. These distinctions prepare a scientifically accurate foundation for the bonding chapter.

questions.question: Why does electronegativity require a bonding context?
questions.answer: Its definition concerns attraction for a shared electron pair, not an isolated atom’s electron-removal or addition process.

questions.question: Does a Pauling electronegativity have kJ mol⁻¹ units?
questions.answer: No. It is a relative dimensionless scale value.

questions.question: Why does electronegativity generally increase across a period?
questions.answer: Effective nuclear attraction rises while size generally decreases, strengthening attraction for bonding electrons.

questions.question: Which atom is δ− in HCl?
questions.answer: Chlorine, because it attracts the shared pair more strongly.

questions.question: Does δ− mean an atom has gained one full electron?
questions.answer: No. It represents partial charge separation within the bond.

questions.question: Why are F/Cl electronegativity and electron-gain comparisons different?
questions.answer: They describe different processes: bonded-pair attraction versus electron addition to isolated gaseous atoms.

questions.question: Are H₂ bonds polar?
questions.answer: No. Identical atoms attract the shared pair equally.
